lesson.title: What a Substance Can Become: Chemical Properties
lesson.summary: This section defines chemical properties as descriptions of how a substance reacts, using iron's rusting reaction as a worked example of bonds rearranging into new compounds.
lesson.body:
Physical properties, covered in the previous section, describe a substance without changing what it fundamentally is. Chemical properties describe the opposite kind of information: how a substance behaves when it reacts, meaning what new substances it can form and under what conditions. Flammability, reactivity with acid, toxicity, and the tendency to rust or tarnish are all chemical properties, and every one of them can only be observed by actually letting the substance undergo, or attempt to undergo, a chemical reaction. You cannot know that hydrogen gas is flammable just by looking at it or weighing it; you find out by exposing it to a spark and watching it react explosively with oxygen. This is the defining feature that separates a chemical property from a physical one: measuring it necessarily transforms the original substance into something chemically different, whereas measuring a physical property, like density or melting point, leaves the original substance intact.

Chemical properties are really statements about how a substance's atoms will rearrange their bonds when they encounter other substances, which connects directly to how compounds were defined earlier in this unit. A compound's formula describes a fixed set of atoms held together by chemical bonds, and a chemical property describes the conditions under which those bonds will break and reform into a different compound. Iron's tendency to rust is a classic example. Iron metal, exposed to oxygen and moisture in the air, undergoes a chemical reaction described by the balanced equation 4Fe + 3O2 to 2Fe2O3, in which four iron atoms combine with three oxygen molecules to form two units of iron(III) oxide, the reddish brown compound commonly called rust. Before the reaction, you have shiny gray metallic iron; after, you have a crumbly reddish compound with an entirely different crystal structure, color, hardness, and density. That transformation, and the fact that it happens at all under ordinary atmospheric conditions, is exactly what chemists mean when they describe iron's chemical property of reactivity toward oxygen.

Not every element or compound shares the same chemical properties, and these differences are often dramatic even among elements that look similar physically. Gold and iron are both shiny, dense metals, but gold strongly resists reacting with oxygen, which is why ancient gold jewelry recovered from shipwrecks still gleams after centuries underwater, while an iron hull from the same wreck corrodes into rust over that same span of time. At the other extreme, sodium and potassium react so readily with water and oxygen that a freshly cut piece of sodium metal visibly tarnishes within seconds of exposure to air. These differences trace back to how tightly each element's atoms hold their outermost electrons, a pattern you began exploring in the elements section and will revisit in later units on bonding.

Chemical properties matter beyond the laboratory, since they determine how substances must be stored and used safely. Knowing that gasoline is flammable, that chlorine gas is toxic, or that concentrated sulfuric acid releases heat when combined with water are all statements of chemical property, each carrying practical consequences, from warning labels to the order in which a chemist mixes acid into water rather than water into acid. Identifying a chemical property, however, always requires that a chemical change actually occur, and it is that broader category, chemical change, that a later section in this unit examines in full detail.
